title: Daily briefing: AI agents sniff out decades-old errors in scientific literature
excerpt: AI can spot errors quickly, but should only be used to check ‘objective’ facts, researchers say. Plus, a Tupperware-sized magnetic-field detector and Gen Z researchers’ tips on building resilience.

• NATURE BRIEFING
  • 10 August 2026

AI can spot errors quickly, but should only be used to check ‘objective’ facts, researchers say. Plus, a Tupperware-sized magnetic-field detector and Gen Z researchers’ tips on building resilience.

By

  • Jacob Smith
  1. Jacob Smith

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Magnetic-field sensor detects brain activity

A new magnetometer — a device used to measure magnetic fields — is sensitive enough to detect the faint signals of the brain’s electrical activity. The technique uses laser beams to track the motions of a tiny levitating magnet suspended in a vacuum chamber. This method is simpler than existing approaches, which require temperatures close to absolute zero or near-perfect shielding from external magnetic interference. The device could be used to detect magnetic fields produced by the brain or heart, and similar levitation techniques could be applied to search for dark matter, researchers say.

Nature | 4 min read

Reference: Science paper

AI spots decades-old scientific errors

Scientists using artificial-intelligence agents to audit the scientific literature have uncovered decades-old errors, from typos to incorrect values in the boiling-point measurements of molecules. The advantage of using AI to fact-check is the speed at which it can scan scientific databases and literature compared with humans, says computer scientist James Zou. But others argue that AI is still prone to mistakes, and its use should be focused on identifying ‘objective’ errors, such as those in calculations, and not assessing how data are interpreted or the novelty of the research.

Nature | 5 min read

More than one million

The number of people living in eastern China who have been evacuated from their homes in the wake of heavy rainfall, flooding and the risk of landslides caused by tropical storm Dolphin. (BBC | 5 min read)

Mutations linked to myriad health benefits

A mutation in a specific gene called FNIP1 is linked to a host of health benefits such as decreased levels of belly fat and blood sugar and a reduced risk of conditions including type 2 diabetes and heart disease. The gene plays a part in cellular metabolism and in how cells detect and respond to certain nutrients. The mutations appear to be rare, but the findings reveal a possible target for drugs that could one day reproduce some of the mutations’ protective effects against cardiometabolic diseases.

Nature | 5 min read

Reference: Nature paper

Infographic of the week

The citations included in patents — documents filed to gain legal protection for potentially money-making inventions — can provide a glimpse of how academic research flows into commercial innovation. Although many papers have obvious importance, some studies in this list are rarely mentioned in academic journals, and even their authors don’t know why they are cited in so many patents. Nonetheless, the analysis does reveal insights about the influence of academia on industry: not least, that the majority of papers most cited in patents are the product of publicly funded research. (Nature | 15 min read) (Source: Nature analysis/relianceonscience.org)

Features & opinion

Universities must address AI cheating

After suspecting that his students cheated on an at-home mid-term exam, economist Robert Serrano held the course’s final examination in person — the class’s average score plummeted. The shock “was not that cheating seems to have occurred on the take-home exam, but how prevalent it appeared to be”, he writes. Universities should establish dedicated committees to ensure academic integrity is upheld, and work as a collective to establish best practices for the appropriate use of AI, to ensure that such tools don’t undermine learning, he argues.

Nature | 5 min read

How Gen Z scientists stay motivated

Geopolitical unrest, rising costs of living, research funding cuts and a widespread sense of decreasing trust in science can make research an uncertain career path for people in Generation Z — those born after 1997. But there are ways to stay motivated and cultivate resilience, four early-career researchers tell Nature. One is to find a research environment that suits your needs, and a support network for the difficult times. Another is to advocate for change from within. “We, as scientists, must support each other and not give up on our careers,” says mycologist Jefferson Reis. “Staying in science is itself a form of resistance.”

Nature | 11 min read

研究人员表示，人工智能可以快速发现错误，但只能用于检查“客观”事实。 另外，还有特百惠大小的磁场探测器和 Z 世代研究人员关于增强弹性的技巧。

磁场传感器检测大脑活动

一种新的磁力计——一种用于测量磁场的设备——足够灵敏，可以检测大脑电活动的微弱信号。 该技术使用激光束来跟踪悬浮在真空室中的微小悬浮磁铁的运动。 这种方法比现有方法更简单，现有方法需要接近绝对零的温度或近乎完美的屏蔽外部磁场干扰。 研究人员表示，该设备可用于检测大脑或心脏产生的磁场，类似的悬浮技术可用于寻找暗物质。

自然 | 4 分钟阅读

参考文献：科学论文

人工智能发现几十年前的科学错误

科学家们使用人工智能代理来审核科学文献，发现了几十年前的错误，从打字错误到分子沸点测量中的错误值。 计算机科学家 James Zou 表示，使用人工智能进行事实核查的优势在于，与人类相比，它扫描科学数据库和文献的速度更快。 但其他人认为人工智能仍然容易出错，其使用应侧重于识别“客观”错误，例如计算中的错误，而不是评估数据的解释方式或研究的新颖性。

自然 | 5 分钟阅读

超过一百万

由于强降雨、洪水和热带风暴“海豚”引发的山体滑坡风险，中国东部地区有多少人从家园撤离。 （BBC | 5 分钟阅读）

突变与无数健康益处相关

一种名为 FNIP1 的特定基因的突变与许多健康益处有关，例如降低腹部脂肪和血糖水平，以及降低患 2 型糖尿病和心脏病等疾病的风险。 该基因在细胞代谢以及细胞如何检测和响应某些营养物质方面发挥着重要作用。 这些突变似乎很罕见，但研究结果揭示了药物的一个可能靶点，有朝一日可以重现一些突变对心脏代谢疾病的保护作用。

自然 | 5 分钟阅读

参考文献：《自然》论文

本周信息图

专利中包含的引文（为潜在赚钱发明获得法律保护而提交的文件）可以让我们了解学术研究如何转化为商业创新。 尽管许多论文具有明显的重要性，但该列表中的一些研究很少在学术期刊中提及，甚至它们的作者也不知道为什么它们被这么多专利引用。 尽管如此，分析确实揭示了学术界对工业界影响的见解：尤其是，专利中引用最多的大多数论文都是公共资助研究的产物。 （《自然》| 15 分钟阅读）（来源：《自然》分析/relianceonscience.org）

特点及意见

大学必须解决人工智能作弊问题

经济学家罗伯特·塞拉诺（Robert Serrano）怀疑学生在家中期中考试作弊后，亲自主持了该课程的期末考试，全班平均分直线下降。 他写道，令人震惊的“并不是带回家的考试中似乎发生了作弊，而是作弊现象似乎如此普遍”。 他认为，大学应该建立专门的委员会来确保学术诚信得到维护，并作为一个集体努力建立适当使用人工智能的最佳实践，以确保这些工具不会破坏学习。

自然 | 5 分钟阅读

Z世代科学家如何保持动力

地缘政治动荡、生活成本上升、研究经费削减以及人们普遍认为对科学的信任度下降，可能使研究成为 Z 一代（1997 年以后出生的人）的不确定职业道路。 但四位早期职业研究人员告诉《自然》杂志，有一些方法可以保持动力并培养韧性。 一是找到适合自己需求的研究环境，以及困难时期的支持网络。 另一个是倡导从内部进行变革。 “作为科学家，我们必须互相支持，不要放弃我们的事业，”真菌学家杰斐逊·里斯说。 “留在科学本身就是一种抵抗。”
